title: FAMILY: Long Dresses, Flowing Hair, and a Brash Attitude
author: Michael Foster
summary: Michael Foster uses an anecdote about a conservatively dressed young woman at his church who posted sensualised pin-up artwork online and responded with defensiveness when corrected to distinguish aesthetic modesty (adopting external markers of conservatism as signals of superiority) from actual modesty (an inward posture of humility). Long dresses and flowing hair can be genuinely good externals, but when adopted apart from inward submission to Christ they become costumes for self-display -- and at that point modesty has been lost even if every inch of skin is covered. Foster cites 1 Peter's call to a gentle and quiet spirit as the biblical foundation for genuine modesty, noting that inward transformation toward Christ naturally produces external modesty over time. He critiques the current modesty-and-femininity discourse for running on comparison before men rather than reverence before God, and concludes he would rather see a woman with genuine inward submission still growing in outward modesty than one who has perfected the external aesthetic while carrying a wild and unsubmissive heart.
points: Aesthetic modesty (external markers as costume) is fundamentally different from actual modesty (inward humility before God).
External trappings adopted without inward transformation become tools for self-display and comparison with others.
Biblical modesty begins in the heart -- the gentle and quiet spirit of 1 Peter is the foundation, not the wardrobe.
Current modesty discourse often substitutes comparison before men for reverence before God, running on rivalry rather than devotion.
Inward submission to Christ naturally produces external modesty over time; the reverse is not reliably true.
quotes: There is a difference between aesthetic modesty and actual modesty.

Some people adopt the outward trappings of conservatism because they are visible and legible... But they can also become costumes, a way of signaling that you are more feminine, more righteous, and more set apart than everyone else around you.
At that point, modesty has already been lost, even if every inch of skin is covered.
Biblical modesty begins in the heart. It is tied to humility, self-possession, and what Scripture calls a gentle and quiet spirit in 1 Peter.

I would far rather see a woman with a gentle and quiet spirit who is still growing in her outward understanding of modesty than a woman who has perfected the external aesthetic while still carrying a wild, unsubmissive heart.
